s1.title: RASIN Integrated Security Center
why.a2: Because security starts from a foundation that never shakes
why.note: Rasana means steadiness and firmness, and that is where our project's name came from. RASIN: protection that stands firm, and trust that never wavers.
s1.tagline: An integrated physical security design that protects information before an unauthorized hand can reach it.
tb.deptVal: Department of Management Information Systems, College of Business Administration, Taif University
s2.lead: A hypothetical center specializing in cybersecurity and information protection.
s2.why: RASIN is a fictional organization born of imagination: a center for information security and digital protection, built around the course subject: information security. It applies the Internet of Things (IoT), the defining technology of our era, and works to protect data and counter digital cyberattacks. Because RASIN's most precious holdings are data no one can see, the project tells how we guard that digital treasure with tools you can touch: a fence and a gate, a camera that never blinks, and a door that opens only for those entitled to enter. Information is protected in the building before it is protected on the network.
s3.explain: Sensitivity rises with height: the higher a person goes, the more verification points they pass through.
cia.c.def: Ensuring that only authorized people can access information.
cia.i.def: Protecting information from unauthorized modification or destruction.
cia.a.def: Ensuring that authorized people can reach information and systems whenever they need them.
cia.c.1: Visitors are kept south of the turnstile line.
cia.c.2: All lifts and stairs sit behind that line.
cia.c.3: The executive meeting room faces the lift, so visitors never see the offices.
cia.c.4: Opaque glazing on the operations-center façade.
cia.i.1: The server room and archive sit behind a mantrap with two-factor verification.
cia.i.2: A single logged point for receiving records.
cia.a.1: A “protected vertical spine”: dry rooms on the ground floor, the server room on the first, the archive on the second — no water pipes.
cia.a.2: An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) room and a backup generator.
s4.c1.title: Physical barriers
s4.c1.w1: A 2.4 m anti-climb fence fitted with a vibration sensor.
s4.c1.w2: Two gates: one for pedestrians, one for vehicles with a hydraulic road blocker.
s4.c1.w3: Fixed bollards in front of the entrance.
s4.c1.w4: Laminated security glass, and bars on the rear ground-floor windows.
s4.c1.where: Along the whole site perimeter (280 m), at both gates, across the entrance forecourt, and on the building façades.
s4.c1.why: The road blocker holds a vehicle until it has been inspected and stops a vehicle-ramming attempt; the vibration cable pinpoints the section being climbed or cut, so the PTZ camera turns to it.
s4.c2.title: Surveillance
s4.c2.w2: Every Z4 room has 80% coverage or more; the server room and archive 100%, the operations center 99%.
s4.c2.where: PTZ cameras on the fence corners, a licence-plate camera at the vehicle gate, a camera facing the turnstiles, and two opposing cameras in the server room and in the archive.
s4.c2.why: Continuous monitoring and recorded evidence of every event; visible cameras deter before they detect. Operations-center cameras capture movement and people, not screen content.
s4.c3.title: Intrusion detection
s4.c3.w1: 24 sensors and alarm buttons: motion detectors, door contacts, glass-break detectors and silent panic buttons.
s4.c3.where: Along the whole fence, ground-floor windows, emergency exits, and the server room and archive; panic buttons at reception, the guard post and the control room.
s4.c3.why: Motion detectors catch any movement outside working hours or without a logged entry; a panic button sends a silent alarm to the control room without the threat noticing.
s4.c4.title: Guarding & screening
s4.c4.w1: 8 guard posts, with a required force of about 34 guards.
s4.c4.w2: A nine-step visitor procedure, and four verification layers before the lobby.
s4.c4.where: Both gate kiosks on the site, staffed around the clock; the entrance, screening and control-room posts on the ground floor; and a mobile patrol around the building and perimeter.
s4.c4.why: The human element verifies, decides and responds where devices are not enough. The four entrance layers: face camera, then the vestibule under the guard's eye, then ID, X-ray and metal detector, then the badge.
s4.c5.title: Access control
s4.c5.w1: 40 points: card readers, two-factor readers, turnstiles and mantraps.
s4.c5.w2: A permissions matrix for nine job roles.
s4.c5.where: Turnstiles on the ground floor, a card reader on every department door, and a mantrap with two two-factor readers in front of the server room and archive.
s4.c5.why: A stolen card alone cannot open a Z4 zone, and the mantrap's second door will not open until the first has closed, so two people cannot enter on one card. Access follows the job, not just the floor.
s4.c6.title: Environmental factors
s4.c6.w2: Perimeter and emergency lighting; ventilation with protected air intakes on the roof.
s4.c6.w3: Dual precision cooling (N+1), a generator and an uninterruptible power supply.
s4.c6.w4: Clean-agent gas suppression and water-leak detection.
s4.c6.where: The server, power and archive rooms; the backup generator in the service yard; air intakes on the roof; lighting on the fence, forecourt and car parks.
s4.c6.why: Clean-agent gas puts out a fire without water, so servers and paper are not damaged. Lighting deters and keeps the cameras effective at night.
s5.ecc.name: Essential Cybersecurity Controls
s5.ecc.scope: National Cybersecurity Authority · Subdomain 2-14 Physical Security
s5.iso.name: Annex A — Physical controls
s5.nist.name: Physical and Environmental Protection family (PE)
ecc.1: Define, document and approve physical protection requirements.
ecc.1.a: Physical protection requirements defined, documented and approved.
ecc.2.a: The fence and its vibration sensor, the road blocker, intrusion detectors, panic buttons and guard posts.
ecc.3: Areas of application: access control to sensitive areas, entry/exit logging and CCTV monitoring, protection of records, secure disposal, and equipment protection.
ecc.3.a: Card and two-factor readers and mantraps; cameras and the licence-plate camera; the media vault; the secure-destruction room; environmental sensors and suppression to protect equipment.
ecc.4.a: Physical protection controls and permission lists reviewed every six months and after any incident.
iso.1.a: The fence and its vibration sensor, both gates, bollards, the road blocker, windows and façades, and perimeter lighting.
iso.2.a: Gate 1, the vestibule and turnstiles, card readers, the licence-plate camera, the metal detector, the X-ray machine and guard posts.
iso.3.a: Steel doors for Z4 zones, two-factor readers, mantraps, and windows and façades.
iso.4.a: Fixed and PTZ cameras; motion, door and glass-break detectors; panic buttons; perimeter lighting; and central monitoring (BMS).
iso.5: Protecting against physical and environmental threats
iso.5.a: Temperature, humidity and water-leak sensors, early smoke detection, clean-agent suppression, ventilation and central monitoring.
iso.6.a: No unescorted visitors in Z4, and a clean-desk policy.
iso.7.a: No documents left on desks after hours, automatic screen lock, and a locked cabinet in every office.
iso.8.a: Precision cooling for technical rooms, and servers in locked racks.
iso.9.a: Laptops are encrypted and logged out and back in through the staff entrance.
iso.10.a: Backups kept in fire-resistant safes in the media vault, with every removal and return logged at the receiving point.
iso.11.a: The backup generator and UPS, precision cooling, ventilation, and the emergency power-off switch.
iso.12.a: Cables run in closed conduits; network ports are disabled in Z1 and Z2.
iso.13.a: Maintenance technicians are escorted inside Z4 zones, and tools are inventoried on entry and exit.
iso.14: Secure disposal or re-use of equipment
iso.14.a: Paper and media are destroyed in the destruction room before leaving, under camera, with a signed destruction record.
pe.3.a: Card and two-factor readers, turnstiles, mantraps, guard posts, the road blocker, and windows and façades.
pe.6.a: Fixed, PTZ and licence-plate cameras, intrusion detectors and panic buttons.
pe.10.a: An emergency power-off switch by the door, with a cover against accidental presses.
pe.11.a: An auto-start backup generator, and a UPS covering servers, the operations center and security systems until the generator runs.
pe.12.a: Battery lighting for corridors and stairs, and illuminated exit signs.
pe.13.a: Smoke detectors, early smoke detection (VESDA), and clean-agent suppression in the server, power and archive rooms.
pe.14.a: Temperature and humidity sensors, precision cooling (N+1), and general ventilation and air-conditioning.
pe.15.a: No water pipes above technical rooms or the archive; leak-detection cables under the server floor and on the archive ceiling.
pe.16.a: An X-ray machine for bags and parcels.

s7.m1: Architecture is the first line of defense.
s7.m1s: Protection begins with the design of the place.
s7.m2: Every piece of information is a trust; every device is a responsibility.
s7.m2s: Data protection is not limited to digital systems; every asset carries value worth protecting.
s7.m3: Physical and information security are one system.
s7.m3s: Protection is never complete with a secure wall or an advanced digital system alone, but with the integration of architectural design and cybersecurity.
s8.link: In the information age, defending the homeland extends to protecting its information and digital assets — which is what the RASIN project applies through the Essential Cybersecurity Controls issued by the National Cybersecurity Authority.
